drills.q: Name the query language for RDF, for Neo4j's property graph, and for TinkerPop-compliant engines.
drills.a: RDF -> SPARQL. Neo4j -> Cypher. TinkerPop (e.g. Neptune, JanusGraph) -> Gremlin.

drills.q: True or false: Amazon Neptune can be self-hosted on-premise.
drills.a: False. Neptune is fully managed only, with no self-hosted option, unlike Neo4j and ArangoDB.

drills.q: What does index-free adjacency claim, and in one sentence, why does a relational JOIN not get the same guarantee?
drills.a: A single-hop traversal is O(1) because each node stores a direct pointer to its adjacent relationships. A relational JOIN's cost scales with the size of the tables being joined and compounds with every additional hop, since each hop is a fresh index lookup, not a stored pointer.

drills.q: A team wants a graph database because 'we have relationships between entities.' What's the first question you'd ask, and why?
drills.a: What's the actual traversal depth and fan-out of the real query pattern? Most 'we need a graph' requirements are shallow and fixed-depth, which a recursive CTE on the existing relational schema handles with no new infrastructure -- the graph model only earns its cost when traversal depth is unpredictable/unbounded and is the primary access pattern.

drills.q: Explain why a 'Country: USA' node connected to every US user is a production problem for a Neo4j-style graph, using the specific mechanism.
drills.a: It's a supernode: traversing from it fans out to millions of relationships, breaking the O(1)-per-hop assumption of index-free adjacency in practice, because even a pointer-walk over millions of edges from one node has real cost. Fix by remodelling (bucket by region) rather than modelling shared attributes as edges to one universal node.

drills.q: Compare Neo4j, Amazon Neptune, and ArangoDB on one axis each: traversal depth, AWS integration, and data-model breadth.
drills.a: Neo4j: deepest traversal-specific optimization and graph-algorithm tooling (GDS). Neptune: deepest native AWS integration (S3, IAM, CloudWatch, SageMaker), fully managed only. ArangoDB: broadest data-model breadth -- document + graph + search + vector in one engine via AQL, at the cost of specialist graph depth.

drills.q: Why does entity resolution stall real knowledge-graph projects more often than entity extraction does?
drills.a: LLMs made extraction cheap, but resolution -- deciding whether 'Bob Smith', 'R. Smith', and an email address are the same entity -- has no clean automated solution and is chronically scoped as a one-time cleanup step, when it's actually an ongoing pipeline stage that reopens with every new data source added.

drills.q: What does GraphRAG add over vector-only RAG, mechanically, and roughly what does full Microsoft-style indexing cost per million tokens?
drills.a: It extracts entities/relationships into a graph, clusters them into communities (Leiden algorithm), and pre-summarizes each community with an LLM, enabling global/cross-corpus questions no single chunk answers. Roughly $20-40 per million tokens of source corpus, a one-time indexing cost.

drills.q: A corpus's query logs show 95% single-document lookups and 5% cross-document synthesis questions. Do you build full GraphRAG? Justify with the cost tradeoff.
drills.a: Generally no -- hybrid search plus reranking already serves the 95% cheaply and well; paying $20-40/million tokens to index the entire corpus to serve a 5% minority is usually the wrong sizing decision unless that 5% carries disproportionate business value, in which case a scoped/lighter (LightRAG-style, ~$0.50/M tokens) approach targeted at just that slice is worth evaluating first.

drills.q: Write the recursive CTE (in words, not full SQL syntax required) that would replace a 'find everyone within 3 hops' graph query on a `follows(follower_id, followee_id)` table, and state the depth guard.
drills.a: A WITH RECURSIVE CTE: base case selects direct followees of the starting user at depth 1; recursive case joins the follows table against the CTE's prior result to find followees-of-followees, incrementing depth; a WHERE depth < 3 guard stops the recursion at 3 hops; final SELECT DISTINCT dedupes users reached via multiple paths.

drills.q: Two ingestion pipelines create the same real-world entity as two different nodes at the same moment. What's the root cause and the fix?
drills.a: A race in upsert-by-external-key logic with no database-level constraint enforcing uniqueness on that key. Fix: a unique constraint on the external key so the second concurrent create fails or merges instead of silently duplicating, plus a periodic reconciliation job to catch near-duplicates entity resolution missed.

drills.q: Why would you explicitly choose ArangoDB over a specialist graph engine for a given workload, and name the one scenario where that choice would be wrong.
drills.a: Choose ArangoDB when the workload is genuinely mixed (documents plus moderate graph traversal), to consolidate three separate systems (document store, graph DB, search engine) into one operational surface with one consistency model. Wrong when the workload is graph-first and graph-heavy -- deep algorithmic traversal, community detection, or centrality analysis at billions of edges -- where a specialist's years of traversal-specific query-planner optimization outperforms a generalist's graph layer.
